name: Great circle
seoDesc: Great circle: work out great circle distance from the latitude and the longitude. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Great circle calculator the latitude and the longitude and it returns great circle distance. Think of it as a shortcut for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Great circle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Great circle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports great circle distance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the hemisphere (E/W) (Coordinates — first point) and the hemisphere (E/W) (Coordinates — second point)); then you type in the latitude (Coordinates — first point), the longitude (Coordinates — first point), the latitude (Coordinates — second point) and the longitude (Coordinates — second point).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Great circle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Temperature 1=the cosine of (((174533 ÷ 10000000) × hemisphere (E ÷ W) × longitude − 174533 ÷ 10000000 × hemisphere (E ÷ W) × longitude))
Hemisphere (N/S)=(10000000 ÷ 174533) × (Temperature 2 ÷ the sine of ((174533 ÷ 10000000) × latitude × hemisphere (N ÷ S))) ÷ latitude
Hemisphere (N/S)=(10000000 ÷ 174533) × (Temperature 3 ÷ the cosine of ((174533 ÷ 10000000) × latitude × hemisphere (N ÷ S))) ÷ latitude
Great circle distance (sphere)=(radius — sphere × (Temperature 2 + Temperature 3 × the cosine of (((174533 ÷ 10000000) × hemisphere (E ÷ W) × longitude − 174533 ÷ 10000000 × hemisphere (E ÷ W) × longitude))))
Great circle distance (ellipsoid)=(latitude, latitude, longitude, longitude, hemisphere (N ÷ S), hemisphere (N ÷ S), hemisphere (E ÷ W), hemisphere (E ÷ W), 1)
Warning=(latitude, latitude, longitude, longitude, hemisphere (N ÷ S), hemisphere (N ÷ S), hemisphere (E ÷ W), hemisphere (E ÷ W), 0)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Coordinates, opening in degrees / minutes / seconds

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Great circle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the latitude and the longitude — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Great circle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns great circle distance, derived from the latitude and the longitude. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Great circle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the latitude and the longitude, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter latitude (Coordinates — first point) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Latitude (Coordinates — first point) opens in degrees / minutes / seconds and the chip beside it offers 4 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Great circle distance (sphere) = 1081220382 km. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Great circle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
